msIdentifier.repository: Beinecke Rare Book & Manuscript Library, Yale University

projectDesc.p: James Joyce's unpublished correspondence, collected, annotated, and made available as a digital edition

div.p: Dear Pound: This is to introduce a good friend of mine Mr Francis Budgen who helped me often and in many ways in Zurich. He is a painter but that is only one of his accomplishments. He is thinking of settling down in London so I thought I ought to repay in some way his kindness to me and my book during my frequent attacks of semiblindness. He is very interested in Ulysses but I shall be satisfied if that serve as means to any end.

div.note: This note is probably the “letter for Pound” that JJ enclosed in his undated letter to Frank Budgen of “(?) September 1920” (LI 144).

JJ met the English painter Frank Spencer Curtis Budgen (1882-1971) in the summer of 1918 when Budgen was working for the British government at the Ministry of Information in Zurich. Budgen tells of meeting JJ at the Zurich pension of the British artist, Horace Taylor (1881-1934), in his book James Joyce and the Making of Ulysses (1934; rpt. Bloomington: Indiana University Press, 1960), 9-15 (see also Ellmann, JJ 429). In August 1920, Budgen visited Paris for a week and was now in London where JJ hoped this note would assist him (LIII 17). JJ was always eager to discuss Ulysses with Budgen, whose intelligence, worldliness, and patient attentiveness helped JJ think through the stylistic and narrative challenges of Ulysses, as Budgen’s indispensable book documents. In this period, JJ wrote Budgen frequently for ideas, suggestions, and even copies of Bits of Fun, a semi-erotic periodical published in London (LI 144). He so thoroughly trusted Budgen to stimulate his creativity that he wrote him in late September 1920: “I am sorry you do not think your ideas on Circe worth sending. As I told you a catchword is enough to set me off” (LI 147). Budgen soon settled in London, married, and remained there for the rest of his life. In earlier years, he had served as national secretary of the British Socialist Labour Party, and had translated the Communist Manifesto into English with Lily G. Aitken and published the edition through the Socialist Labour Party circa 1908. For that period of his life, see his book Myselves When Young (New York: Oxford University Press, 1970), 72-102. Budgen lived long enough to meet Joyce scholars, and was a guest of honor at the first Joyce symposium in 1967. In his introduction to James Joyce and the Making of Ulysses, Hugh Kenner praises Budgen’s critical approach as “unpretentious, reliable, highly animated,” skillful in avoiding “irrelevant ideas generated by the technical novelties of Joyce’s text,” and infused with a “wholly unembarrassed awareness of Joyce as a human being” (ix-xiii).
For JJ’s glaucoma and initial eye surgery, see JJ to Pound, 5 June 1917; 20 August 1917; 20 August 1917 (SL 226-27).
